title: Benford's Law: Why the Number 1 Comes First
question: Why do about 30% of real-world numbers begin with the digit 1, and only 5% with 9?
summary: A worn book of logarithm tables led to one of mathematics' strangest regularities. Scale invariance explains it, multiplicative growth produces it, and fraud investigators use it.
content:
Take any large collection of real-world numbers: the populations of every town on Earth, the lengths of rivers, stock prices, the street addresses in a phone book, the physical constants in a textbook. Look only at the first digit of each. Intuition says each digit from 1 to 9 should lead about one ninth of the time. Instead, about 30% of the numbers start with 1, about 18% with 2, and fewer than 5% with 9. This strange regularity is called Benford's Law, and it hides a surprisingly deep idea about scale.

A Discovery in Worn Pages

In 1881 the astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed that the early pages of his book of logarithm tables were far more worn than the later ones. People were looking up numbers starting with 1 much more often than numbers starting with 9. He wrote a two-page note proposing the rule, and it was forgotten. In 1938 the physicist Frank Benford rediscovered it and tested it on over 20,000 numbers from 20 different sources, from baseball statistics to molecular weights. The law held almost everywhere, and it took his name.

The Formula

The probability that the leading digit is d is log10(1 + 1/d). For d = 1 that is log10(2), about 30.1%; for d = 9 it is log10(10/9), about 4.6%. The logarithm is the clue. Benford's Law says that the logarithms of the numbers, not the numbers themselves, are spread evenly. On a logarithmic ruler, the stretch from 1 to 2 is much longer than the stretch from 9 to 10, so more numbers land there.

Why Scale Invariance Forces It

Here is the beautiful argument. Suppose there were a universal law for the first digits of, say, river lengths. That law should not depend on whether we measure in kilometres or miles, because nature does not know our units. Multiplying every number by a constant must leave the digit distribution unchanged. Roger Pinkham showed in 1961 that the only distribution of leading digits with this scale invariance is exactly Benford's. Any other pattern would change when you switched units.

A second explanation, given by Theodore Hill in 1995, is even more general: if you mix together numbers drawn from many different distributions, the result tends toward Benford's Law. That is why a grab-bag like the numbers on a newspaper's front page fits it so well.

When It Fails

Benford's Law is not universal. It fails for numbers confined to a narrow range (human heights in metres all start with 1 or 2), for assigned numbers (phone numbers, ZIP codes), and for data with built-in caps or minimums. It works best for quantities that span several orders of magnitude and arise from multiplicative processes, such as growth, compounding, and the products of many random factors.

Catching Fraud

The law has a practical edge. When people invent numbers, they tend to spread first digits too evenly and avoid repeating digits. Forensic accountants, following Mark Nigrini's work in the 1990s, routinely test expense reports and tax returns against Benford's distribution; large deviations flag accounts for closer inspection. It has been applied to election returns and scientific data as well, though with caution: a mismatch is a reason to look, never proof of wrongdoing, and misapplying the test to data that shouldn't follow the law has produced many false alarms.

What It Teaches

Benford's Law is a reminder that "random" is not one thing. Our intuition assumes uniform randomness, but much of the world is generated by multiplication rather than addition, and multiplication naturally lives on a logarithmic scale. The worn pages in Newcomb's book were a fingerprint of how the universe grows things.

perspectives.title: Mathematics
perspectives.description: Benford's Law is the unique leading-digit distribution invariant under changes of scale; it follows from logarithms being uniformly distributed modulo 1.

perspectives.title: Physics
perspectives.description: Nature has no preferred units, so any universal law about measured quantities must be scale invariant, the same reasoning that underlies dimensional analysis.

perspectives.title: Statistics
perspectives.description: Hill's theorem shows that mixtures of many distributions converge toward Benford, explaining why heterogeneous data sets fit it so well.

perspectives.title: Forensic Accounting
perspectives.description: Fabricated numbers tend to deviate from Benford's distribution, making it a useful screening tool, though one that requires care about when the law should apply.

perspectives.title: Cognitive Psychology
perspectives.description: People's intuitive sense of randomness is uniform and additive, which is exactly why invented data betrays itself and why the law feels so surprising.

openQuestions: Why do some data sets that span many orders of magnitude still deviate systematically from Benford's Law?
Could a sufficiently sophisticated fraudster always evade digit-based detection, and what would be the next statistical fingerprint?
Do the leading digits of mathematical sequences (like powers of 2 or Fibonacci numbers) following Benford reveal something about the physical world, or only about logarithms?
Are there analogous hidden regularities in other properties of real-world data that we have not yet noticed?
